title: Good Governance Principles in Administrative Law

content.overview: Good governance principles — transparency, accountability, participation, responsiveness, fairness and integrity — inform modern administrative law and reinforce constitutional standards of non-arbitrariness and fairness.
content.glance: List the relevant good-governance principles; link each to a concrete administrative-law doctrine (RTI, reasoned orders, natural justice, judicial review); apply to the decision under challenge.
content.study: Good governance is not a free-standing cause of action, but its principles are operationalised through existing doctrines: transparency through RTI and publication requirements; accountability through judicial review and audit; fairness through natural justice; integrity through conflict-of-interest rules. Indian courts increasingly refer to good-governance values when interpreting Article 14 and statutory duties. Current-law framing: treat good governance as interpretive support for constitutional and statutory standards, not as an independent source of power.

sections.heading: Transparency
sections.body: Access to information and publication of reasons support accountable administration.

sections.heading: Accountability
sections.body: Judicial review, audit and institutional oversight hold decision-makers to legal standards.

sections.heading: Participation and Responsiveness
sections.body: Consultation and consideration of affected interests improve legitimacy and quality of decisions.

sections.heading: Fairness and Integrity
sections.body: Natural justice and conflict-of-interest rules operationalise fairness and integrity.

sections.heading: Legal Status
sections.body: Good-governance principles reinforce but do not replace constitutional and statutory duties.

examples.title: Opaque allocation
examples.body: A public resource is allocated without published criteria or reasons. Transparency and Article 14 non-arbitrariness are both engaged.

examples.title: Unreasoned order
examples.body: An authority rejects an application with a one-line order. The duty to give reasons (speaking orders) operationalises accountability and fairness.

hypotheticals.question: Is good governance an independent enforceable right?
hypotheticals.analysis: Not as a free-standing right; it is given effect through existing constitutional and statutory doctrines.

hypotheticals.question: Does transparency require disclosure of every internal deliberation?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Legitimate confidentiality and deliberative privilege may limit disclosure; RTI exemptions illustrate the balance.

distinctions.title: Good-governance values vs operative legal doctrines
distinctions.right: Enforceable doctrines (RTI, natural justice, judicial review)

misconceptions.trap: Good governance creates new free-standing causes of action.
misconceptions.correction: It reinforces existing constitutional and statutory standards.
Legitimate confidentiality limits apply; balance is required.

cases.name: Tata Cellular v Union of India
cases.ratioDecidendi: Courts review legality and rationality of the process.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a good-governance problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Identify the governance principle engaged. II. Link it to the operative doctrine. III. Apply the doctrine to the facts. IV. Conclude.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should submissions contain?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Principle identified; linked doctrine; factual application; precise relief.

bareActPointers: RTI Act where transparency is engaged
examTips: Link every governance value to a concrete doctrine.
Do not plead good governance as a free-standing right.
